title: Before the Feed: How the Web Became Personal
description: Six stops from the shared family computer to handmade homepages, screen names, portals, and search.

stops.title: The family computer becomes a portal
stops.curatorText: The early web did not arrive in a pocket. It arrived in one shared room, on one glowing CRT, through a phone line everybody else still needed. The family computer turned going online into a household negotiation and made the screen feel like a doorway.
stops.detail: AOL discs and setup wizards made access feel consumer-friendly, but the experience was still physical: mailers, modem sounds, mouse pads, printed passwords, and time limits.

stops.title: Mosaic gives the web a visual front door
stops.curatorText: The first website looked like lab notes. Mosaic helped the same linked-document idea become something people could see themselves exploring: gray window chrome, blue links, and images sitting inside the page.
stops.detail: The change was not instant mass adoption. It was a shift in imagination—the web started looking like a place rather than a protocol.

stops.title: GeoCities turns pages into rooms
stops.curatorText: Personal homepages were part diary, part fan shrine, and part self-invention project. Their rough edges were evidence that a person had chosen every color, GIF, link, and sentence.
stops.detail: GeoCities neighborhoods supplied a loose map while human-curated directories helped visitors find the next handmade corner.

stops.title: Guestbooks, counters, and Webrings leave traces
stops.curatorText: A counter said somebody had arrived. A guestbook showed who stayed long enough to leave a note. A Webring trusted one small site to point toward another.
stops.detail: These tiny objects made the web feel inhabited and gave discovery a visible human chain instead of an invisible ranking system.

stops.title: Screen names make presence personal
stops.curatorText: Buddy lists and away messages turned identity into something you edited in public. A screen name, a lyric, and an ASCII heart could communicate mood, availability, and belonging.
stops.detail: The page stopped being the only place you performed a self online. Presence moved into a live social layer that followed the rest of pop culture home.

stops.title: Portals and search begin sorting the neighborhood
stops.curatorText: By the late 1990s, the web was too large to navigate only by hand. Portals bundled news, mail, search, and identity into a starting screen while cleaner search tools promised a faster route through the noise.
stops.detail: The handmade web did not disappear overnight, but the center of gravity shifted from choosing a neighbor to querying an index—the beginning of the road toward today's feed-shaped internet.
